mcqs.q: The clinical classification of pulpal & periapical diseases used here is based on the:
mcqs.explain: The terminology and classification are based on those suggested by the American Association of Endodontists in 2012.

mcqs.q: 'Pulpitis' is a term denoting:
mcqs.explain: Pulpitis denotes inflammation of the dental pulp — clinically reversible/irreversible, histologically acute/chronic/hyperplastic.

mcqs.q: A clinically NORMAL pulp gives which response to cold testing?
opts: A mild/transient response lasting 1–2 seconds after the stimulus is removed
mcqs.explain: A clinically normal pulp gives a mild or transient response to cold, lasting no more than one to two seconds after the stimulus is removed.

mcqs.q: When pulp testing, you should first test:
opts: Adjacent and contralateral teeth as a baseline
A tooth in the other arch at random
mcqs.explain: Test adjacent and contralateral teeth first so the patient becomes familiar with a normal response and a baseline is established.

mcqs.q: 'Reversible pulpitis' is characterised by inflammation that:
opts: Resolves, returning the pulp to normal
mcqs.explain: In reversible pulpitis the inflammation should resolve and the pulp return to normal; discomfort reverses quickly after the irritant is removed.

mcqs.q: Which is a causative factor of reversible pulpitis?
opts: Caries, exposed dentin, or a defective restoration
mcqs.explain: Causes of reversible pulpitis include caries, exposed dentin, recent dental treatment and defective restorations.

mcqs.q: The treatment of reversible pulpitis is:
mcqs.explain: Conservative removal of the irritant resolves the symptoms of reversible pulpitis.

mcqs.q: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis classically produces, on cold testing:
opts: Heightened, prolonged pain that lingers after the stimulus is removed
mcqs.explain: Cold elicits heightened and prolonged episodes of pain that linger even after the thermal stimulus is removed.

mcqs.q: Irreversible pulpitis is defined as a:
opts: Vital, inflamed pulp that is incapable of healing
Pulp that always heals on its own
mcqs.explain: Irreversible pulpitis is a vital inflamed pulp that is incapable of healing.

mcqs.q: If symptomatic irreversible pulpitis is left untreated, the pulp will eventually:
mcqs.explain: When symptomatic irreversible pulpitis remains untreated, the pulp will eventually become necrotic.

mcqs.q: Asymptomatic irreversible pulpitis differs from the symptomatic form in that the patient:
opts: Has no symptoms despite the pulp being unable to heal
mcqs.explain: In asymptomatic irreversible pulpitis the vital inflamed pulp cannot heal, but the patient does not complain of symptoms (e.g. deep caries silently reaching the pulp).

mcqs.q: 'Pulp necrosis' indicates:
mcqs.explain: Pulp necrosis indicates the death of the dental pulp.

mcqs.q: A necrotic pulp typically:
opts: Does NOT respond to pulp testing
mcqs.explain: A necrotic pulp is usually non-responsive to pulp testing — the blood supply is absent and the nerves are non-functional.

mcqs.q: In a multirooted tooth, pulp necrosis may be confusing because:
opts: It can be partial — one canal may respond while another does not
mcqs.explain: Necrosis may be partial or complete; in a multirooted tooth one root may give no response while another gives a positive response.

mcqs.q: Pulp necrosis with no caries, restorations or luxation is most likely caused by:
opts: A longitudinal (cracked-tooth) fracture extending into the pulp
mcqs.explain: In the absence of restorations, caries or luxation injuries, necrosis is likely caused by a longitudinal fracture extending from the occlusal surface into the pulp.

mcqs.q: A tooth that has been endodontically treated with obturated canals is classified as:
mcqs.explain: 'Previously treated' indicates the tooth is endodontically treated and the canals are obturated; no vital/necrotic tissue remains to respond to testing.

mcqs.q: A tooth that had a pulpotomy or pulpectomy (partial endodontics) is classified as:
mcqs.explain: 'Previously initiated therapy' indicates partial endodontic therapy (e.g. pulpotomy, pulpectomy); an accurate pulpal diagnosis is no longer possible.

mcqs.q: NORMAL apical tissues show, radiographically:
opts: An intact lamina dura and uniform PDL space
mcqs.explain: Normal apical tissues are not sensitive to percussion/palpation; the lamina dura is intact and the PDL space is uniform.

mcqs.q: Symptomatic apical periodontitis produces:
opts: A painful response to biting, percussion or palpation
mcqs.explain: Symptomatic apical periodontitis is inflammation of the apical periodontium producing a painful response to biting, percussion or palpation; radiographs show at least a widened PDL space.

mcqs.q: Asymptomatic apical periodontitis appears radiographically as:
opts: An apical radiolucency, with no clinical symptoms
mcqs.explain: Asymptomatic apical periodontitis is inflammation/destruction of the apical periodontium of pulpal origin, seen as an apical radiolucency, producing no symptoms.

mcqs.q: Asymptomatic apical periodontitis usually responds to pulp vitality tests how?
opts: It does NOT respond (pulp is non-vital)
mcqs.explain: Asymptomatic apical periodontitis does not usually respond to pulp vitality tests, as it is of pulpal (necrotic) origin.

mcqs.q: Acute apical abscess is characterised by:
opts: Rapid onset, spontaneous pain, pus formation and swelling
mcqs.explain: Acute apical abscess is an inflammatory reaction to pulpal infection/necrosis with rapid onset, spontaneous pain, tenderness to pressure, pus formation and swelling.

mcqs.q: A patient with an acute apical abscess may also present with:
opts: Fever and tender cervical/submandibular lymph nodes
mcqs.explain: The patient is frequently febrile, and the cervical and submandibular lymph nodes may be tender; the tooth does not respond to vitality tests and shows mobility.

mcqs.q: Chronic apical abscess is distinguished by:
opts: Intermittent pus discharge through an associated sinus tract
mcqs.explain: Chronic apical abscess has gradual onset, little/no discomfort, and intermittent discharge of pus through an associated sinus tract.

mcqs.q: What clinically distinguishes a chronic apical abscess from asymptomatic apical periodontitis?
opts: The presence of a draining sinus tract
mcqs.explain: Both are asymptomatic with an apical radiolucency, but the chronic apical abscess exhibits intermittent drainage through an associated sinus tract.

mcqs.q: Compared with reversible pulpitis, irreversible pulpitis pain typically:
opts: Lingers after the stimulus is removed
Stops the instant the stimulus is removed
mcqs.explain: Reversible-pulpitis discomfort reverses quickly; irreversible-pulpitis pain is heightened and lingers after the stimulus is removed.

mcqs.q: A necrotic tooth may be hypersensitive to HEAT and relieved by COLD because:
opts: Fluids/gases in the canal expand with heat and extend into periapical tissues
mcqs.explain: Remnant fluids or gases in the pulp canal expand with heat and extend into the periapical tissues, causing heat hypersensitivity often relieved by cold.

mcqs.q: Asymptomatic irreversible pulpitis should be treated:
mcqs.explain: Endodontic treatment should be performed as soon as possible so that symptomatic irreversible pulpitis or necrosis (with severe pain) does not develop.

mcqs.q: For percussion and palpation testing, the baseline should be established using:
mcqs.explain: As with pulp testing, comparative percussion/palpation testing should always begin with normal teeth as a baseline for the patient.

mcqs.q: Advanced irreversible pulpitis may show, radiographically:
opts: Thickening of the periodontal ligament and pulp-space calcification
mcqs.explain: With advanced irreversible pulpitis a thickened PDL may appear, with evidence of pulpal irritation such as pulp chamber/root canal calcification; periradicular bone often shows minimal change.

saqs.q: Classify the diseases of the pulp.
saqs.a: 1) Normal pulp, 2) Reversible pulpitis, 3) Irreversible pulpitis (symptomatic & asymptomatic), 4) Pulp necrosis, 5) Previously treated, 6) Previously initiated therapy.

Reversible: inflammation resolves, the pulp returns to normal, and discomfort reverses quickly after the irritant is removed. Irreversible: a vital inflamed pulp incapable of healing, with prolonged pain that lingers after a (cold) stimulus; left untreated it becomes necrotic.

saqs.q: List the clinical features of pulp necrosis.
saqs.a: Death of the pulp; usually non-responsive to pulp testing (no blood supply, non-functional nerves); may be hypersensitive to heat and relieved by cold; may be partial or complete; radiographically PDL thickening → periapical radiolucency.

saqs.q: Classify the diseases of the apical (periapical) region.
saqs.a: 1) Normal apical tissues, 2) Symptomatic apical periodontitis, 3) Asymptomatic apical periodontitis, 4) Acute apical abscess, 5) Chronic apical abscess.

saqs.q: Differentiate symptomatic from asymptomatic apical periodontitis.
saqs.a: Symptomatic: painful to biting/percussion/palpation; radiograph shows at least a widened PDL space (may/may not respond to vitality tests). Asymptomatic: no symptoms, an apical radiolucency of pulpal origin, and no response to vitality tests.

saqs.q: Describe the features of an acute apical abscess.
saqs.a: An inflammatory reaction to pulpal infection/necrosis with rapid onset, spontaneous pain, tenderness to pressure, pus formation and swelling (intra-oral & facial). Often febrile with tender lymph nodes; no response to vitality tests, with mobility.

saqs.q: Describe a chronic apical abscess and how it is distinguished from asymptomatic apical periodontitis.
saqs.a: A reaction to pulpal infection/necrosis with gradual onset, little/no discomfort and intermittent pus discharge through a sinus tract (apical radiolucency; no vitality response). It is distinguished from asymptomatic apical periodontitis by its draining sinus tract.
